subsystems.name: Scaffold
subsystems.role: a stable, biocompatible body that holds the other parts in a fixed geometry.

subsystems.name: Recognition layer
subsystems.role: decides what is healthy tissue and what is a target, using molecules that bind specific signatures.

subsystems.name: Effector head
subsystems.role: does the actual repair or destruction once the target is confirmed.
parts: drug payload in a release mechanism

subsystems.name: Delivery and transport
subsystems.role: gets the machine to the right cell inside a living body.
parts: surface coating to evade immune clearance

subsystems.name: Power and control
subsystems.role: supplies energy and a way to steer or switch the device off.
parts: chemical fuel or ATP from the host cell

subsystems.name: Safety and clearance
subsystems.role: ensures the device degrades and leaves the body.
parts: molecular size tuned below kidney filtration limit

buildSteps.title: Pick the target signature
buildSteps.detail: Identify a molecular difference — a surface receptor, a mutant protein, a DNA sequence — that appears on diseased cells and not on healthy ones.

buildSteps.title: Design the logic
buildSteps.detail: Encode recognition as binding events that must happen in combination, so the device only acts when several markers match at once.

buildSteps.title: Choose the scaffold
buildSteps.detail: DNA origami gives programmable geometry at roughly 100 nanometre scale; protein cages and polymers are alternatives with different immune behaviour.

buildSteps.title: Attach the effector
buildSteps.detail: Couple a nuclease, protease or drug to the scaffold, often through a linker that only breaks inside the target cell.

buildSteps.title: Assemble and purify
buildSteps.detail: Self-assembly in solution, then separation of correctly built devices from incomplete ones — the hardest quality-control step.

buildSteps.title: Test in cells
buildSteps.detail: Measure targeting accuracy, off-target editing and toxicity in cultured human cells.

buildSteps.title: Test in animals
buildSteps.detail: Assess how long the device survives in blood, where it accumulates, and whether the immune system attacks it.

buildSteps.title: Prove safe clearance
buildSteps.detail: Show that the device and its breakdown products are excreted rather than accumulating in liver or kidney.

buildSteps.title: Human trials and manufacture
buildSteps.detail: Only after all of the above would clinical testing and reproducible large-scale production be attempted — neither has happened for an autonomous molecular surgeon.

prerequisites.why: the 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry recognised molecular motors and switches, but these are far simpler than a repair device and work mainly in solution, not in tissue.
antibody-drug conjugates and engineered immune cells already reach selected cells in patients, though with limited precision.

prerequisites.tech: Precise genome editing inside the body
prerequisites.why: CRISPR-based editors work in cells and some are in trials, but delivering them safely and specifically to a chosen organ remains unsolved.

prerequisites.tech: Power and propulsion at the nanoscale in tissue
prerequisites.why: there is no practical onboard engine; devices must ride diffusion and blood flow, which gives almost no control over destination.

prerequisites.tech: Real-time sensing and control in the body
prerequisites.why: no method yet reports what an individual device is doing deep inside a patient, so autonomy would have to be trusted blind.
nanoparticles can be made degradable, but long-term immune and accumulation behaviour is still poorly predicted.

pathway.milestone: nanoparticle and antibody-drug delivery that concentrates payloads in tumours
pathway.unlocks: real clinical experience with targeting, dosing and clearance.

pathway.milestone: in-body gene editors delivered to a single organ
pathway.unlocks: proof that a molecular tool can be aimed at a specific tissue and act only there.

pathway.milestone: devices that sense a molecular marker and respond by releasing a drug — a closed loop without human control
pathway.unlocks: the first genuinely conditional, autonomous behaviour in a patient.

pathway.milestone: multi-part machines that both recognise and repair, then degrade harmlessly
pathway.unlocks: targeted correction of genetic damage, if control and safety can be demonstrated.

pathway.milestone: factory-built, quality-controlled fleets of medical nanomachines
pathway.unlocks: routine cellular repair — an engineering programme, not a near-term product.
